title: Quantum Mechanics
intro: The quantum mechanics that quantum reservoir computing runs on: state vectors, measurement, qubits and their rotations, time evolution under a Hamiltonian, many-qubit systems, entanglement and mixed states. Each page ends by naming the QRC pages that use it.

blocks.text: The Quantum Reservoir Computing shelf (#/qrc) assumes you can read $\vert\psi\rangle$, know what $\langle Z\rangle$ means and why it needs many shots, can picture a qubit on the Bloch sphere, know that $U = e^{-iHt}$ is how a Hamiltonian moves a state, and are comfortable with tensor products, partial traces and density matrices. This shelf builds exactly that, in the notation the QRC pages use, with a short numpy sample on every page so you can check each claim yourself.

It is a working course, not a survey. Potential wells, the hydrogen atom and scattering are left out, not because they are unimportant but because QRC never uses them. What is in is finite-dimensional quantum mechanics (qubits and spins), plus one infinite-dimensional system, the harmonic oscillator, because continuous-variable reservoirs are built from it.

items: States: a closed system is described by a unit vector $\vert\psi\rangle$ in a complex vector space (a Hilbert space). Vectors that differ only by an overall phase are the same state.
Observables: every measurable quantity is a Hermitian operator $A$; the possible results are its eigenvalues.

Measurement (the Born rule): measuring $A$ gives eigenvalue $a$ with probability $\Vert\Pi_a\vert\psi\rangle\Vert^2$, where $\Pi_a$ projects onto the eigenvectors with that eigenvalue, and leaves the state in $\Pi_a\vert\psi\rangle$, renormalised.

Dynamics: between measurements the state evolves by the Schrödinger equation $i\,\tfrac{d}{dt}\vert\psi\rangle = H\vert\psi\rangle$, so $\vert\psi(t)\rangle = e^{-iHt}\vert\psi(0)\rangle$ (units with $\hbar = 1$, as on every page here).
Composite systems: the state space of two systems is the tensor product of their spaces, so dimensions multiply.

blocks.text: Everything else, mixed states and channels included, follows from these five once you allow yourself to ignore part of a larger system. That last step is where the QRC shelf's Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems) picks up.

items: Foundations (#/quantum/foundations): the linear algebra, state vectors and Dirac notation, measurement and the Born rule, observables, expectation values and uncertainty.
Qubits (#/quantum/qubits): the Bloch sphere, Pauli operators and rotations, gates and circuits including the two-CNOT $XX$ rotation and Trotter steps.
Dynamics (#/quantum/dynamics): the Schrödinger equation, precession and Rabi oscillation, the Heisenberg picture and conserved quantities, the harmonic oscillator.
Many Qubits (#/quantum/many-body): tensor products, entanglement and reduced states, mixed states, and the spin models QRC reservoirs are built from.

blocks.text: Read the pages in order; each assumes the ones before it. Then go to Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels), which starts where Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states) ends, and from there to The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir). If you already know some quantum mechanics, the quickest check is the problems at the foot of each page: if they are easy, skip ahead.

Units: every page sets $\hbar = 1$, so energies and frequencies are measured in the same units and $e^{-iHt}$ needs no constant. Qubit convention: $\vert0\rangle$ has $Z = +1$ and $\vert1\rangle$ has $Z = -1$, and in a register the leftmost tensor factor is qubit 1, exactly as on the QRC pages.
